Typical turbine-inlet temperatures are around 1650 K (2500°F) or higher.
Typical heat fluxes in turbine blades are of the order of 5.5 x 10^6 watts per square meter.
Typical wall-to-coolant temperature ratios in turbine blades are of the order of 2.5 to 1.
Rotational speeds for large gas turbines are around 17,000 rpm, and for small turbines around 65,000 rpm.
Acceleration levels for large gas turbines are around 75,000 g's, and for small turbines around 400,000 g's.
The Dittus-Boelter correlation has remained a favorite for predicting heat transfer in turbine blade cooling passages.
Experimental data showed the Dittus-Boelter correlation overpredicted heat transfer in a square duct by about 50%.
The heat transfer coefficient was found to decrease as the wall-to-bulk temperature ratio increased.
Pressure drop can be greater than predicted for constant property conditions due to variable fluid properties.
Coriolis forces generate secondary flows within the cooling passages at high rotation speeds.
Free-convection heat transfer can become significant at high centrifugal forces and density gradients.
A 10% inaccuracy in the coolant-side heat transfer coefficient can lead to a ±27°F uncertainty in blade metal temperature.
Turbine blade cooling passages often have non-fully developed velocity profiles and noncircular cross-sections.
The literature review covers both analytical and experimental studies on forced-convection heat transfer.
Correlations have been developed to account for the effects of variable fluid properties on heat transfer and pressure drop.
